newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Ex-Soviet states fuel dream of Uighur independence.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet states fuel dream of Uighur independence.

text.p: A clutch of new states bordering China's turbulent Xinjiang province have fuelled ethnic Uighurs' dreams of independence, but diplomats said on Wednesday that the former Soviet republics were unlikely to push their cause.
The Uighur separatists' campaign of shootings and bombings to secure independence attracts none of the concern lavished on equally troubled Tibet.

But reports trickling out about the latest bloody rioting in Xinjiang by the Moslem, Turkic-speaking Uighurs against their Chinese rulers -- sparked, say Uighur exile groups, by Chinese executions of Uighurs last week -- show the northwestern province to be a potential ethnic powder keg.

Gauging the extent of unrest in Xinjiang remains as hard as when Peter Fleming, buccaneering correspondent for the London Times, travelled the region on horseback in the 1930s, a rifle strapped to his saddle for use against yaks and bears.

"In 1935, Sinkiang, if you substitute political for physical difficulties, shared with the peak of Everest the blue riband of inaccessibility," Fleming wrote of the region, a tract of mountain and inhospitable desert five times the size of California.

But the appearance of three independent states on its western border following the Soviet collapse in 1991 -- Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan -- has created a new information channel which piggy-backs on cross-border trade.

Beijing imposed tougher border controls in May last year, saying it wanted to stop the flow of arms to the Uighur separatists. But there are air and rail links between the Kazakh capital Almaty and Xinjiang's regional centre, Urumqi.
The new states also form a powerful well-spring for Uighur separatist hopes.

"The appearance of these republics, despite all their problems, has had a very strong influence," said Kakharman Khozhamberdi, president of the Kazakhstan-based Uighur Association. "It has revolutionised the (separatist) movement."
Khozhamberdi said the Uighurs' strong cultural links with the Central Asian republics made their new-found independence even more potent for the Uighurs.
"We both speak a Turkic language, we are both Moslems, we share a nomadic heritage," he said.

Uighurs remember a Turkic state created in the late 1940s in southeastern Xinjiang by rebellious Kazakhs, Uighurs and Mongols. The shortlived republic's pale blue flag, emblazoned with a white star and crescent, was perched on Khozhamberdi's desk.
"Right of assembly is denied, but Uighur separatism is kept alive and preached in the mosques," he said.
But Western diplomats say the Central Asian states have much to lose in any confrontation with China over Xinjiang.
"Viability of borders is the main problem," said one diplomat. "When you start chipping away at those, it opens up a whole number of problems for the whole region."
He said that questioning China's borders risked questions being asked of their own haphazard and ethnically tense frontiers.
There has been no official Kazakh comment on the riots, which Chinese officials say caused 10 deaths and wounded 144.
Observers say an agreement on reducing border forces in the region between Russia, China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan will be signed in April as planned.
But exiled nationalists say the Uighurs have lost patience with what it calls Beijing's policy of "assimilation" and what they view as their unfair treatment.
They say the recent granting of a three-day spring holiday to Chinese cadres while only one day's holiday was granted for a Moslem festival caused particular ire.

"In East Turkestan (Xinjiang), we've talked with the Chinese for 45 years and we've already said all we could," said Yusupbek Mukhlisi, leader of the separatist United National Revolutionary Front of East Turkestan, which advocates armed struggle. "The Uighurs will use their human right to defend themselves."
